passage: The rain had stopped the buses, and Nandini had missed her stop at the crowded market. Her phone was dead. A tea seller, Sunaina, saw her standing under the awning and lent her a phone to call home. Sunaina's own customers were waiting, but she waited too. When Nandini's father arrived on his scooter, Nandini tugged his sleeve. "Papa, she helped me." She went back to the tea stall and said, "Thank you, Aunty," and then, because it seemed too small, she took a small drawing from her bag. It was of a tea kettle with steam. "I made it while waiting," she said. Sunaina held it up and smiled.

qa.q: What did Sunaina lend Nandini?
qa.a: Sunaina lent her a phone to call home.

qa.q: Why did Nandini give Sunaina a drawing after saying thank you, and what might she have felt?
qa.a: She felt the words alone seemed too small for the help, so she wanted to show real thanks. She likely felt grateful and relieved after being stuck in the rain.

qa.q: What could Nandini do later to show her thanks more?
qa.a: She could return to the stall another day to say thank you again, or write a note, so Sunaina knows the help mattered.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel about the drawing?
qa.a: Sunaina had customers waiting yet helped anyway, so the drawing may show her that the effort was noticed, and she smiled.

grounding: A child thanks a stranger for help with a small gift, showing that real gratitude is more than a rote phrase.

passage: On Friday afternoon, Noor brought Thomas a folded card at the end of the school day in Nairobi. Thomas had spent an hour helping her with a fraction problem that had made her cry the day before. On the card she had drawn a pencil holding a small flag that said "7/8", the answer they had found together. Inside she wrote, "Thank you for not telling me the answer. You made me find it myself." Thomas read it twice, ears turning pink. "You did the work," he said. Noor grinned. "I know, but you waited." She helped him tidy his desk without being asked.

qa.q: What answer did Noor draw on the flag?
qa.a: She drew "7/8" on the small flag.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she wrote the card, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt grateful, and the details show it: she drew the answer they found and thanked him for waiting. Her helping him tidy up without being asked shows she wanted to return the kindness.

qa.q: What could Thomas do to help another classmate who is stuck?
qa.a: He could do as he did with Noor, wait and guide with questions, so the classmate finds the answer with his support.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel receiving the card?
qa.a: Thomas seems moved and a little shy, with pink ears. He may feel proud that the way he helped mattered.

grounding: A child writes a thank-you card and returns a favour, feeling thankful and showing effort behind the gesture.

passage:
"Noor, your bag strap is fixed. Vasudha Aunty came over after dinner and sewed it."
"Oh. Thanks." Noor didn't look up from the TV.
"Just 'oh, thanks'?" Ammi held up the bag. "Look properly."
Noor looked. The strap had been sewn with tiny, even stitches, and a patch of green cloth covered the tear. "She used thread the same colour as the bag."
"She found it in her old tin. Her eyes are weak now. It took her an hour under the tube light."
Noor was quiet. "An hour? For my bag?"
"Mm."
Noor put on her slippers. "Ammi, can I take her some of the kheer?"
"What will you say?"
"I'll tell her about the green patch. And that I don't have to carry my books in my arms anymore."

qa.q: What colour was the cloth that covered the tear?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: How did Noor's feelings change after looking closely at the bag?
qa.a: At first Noor felt nothing much and gave a quick thanks, but seeing the tiny stitches and hearing it took an hour made Noor feel touched and grateful.

qa.q: What helped Noor move from a rote thank-you to real gratitude?
qa.a: Ammi pointed out the effort behind the repair, and Noor chose to take kheer and name exactly what Aunty had done.

qa.q: How might Vasudha Aunty feel when Noor mentions the green patch?
qa.a: She would likely feel appreciated and warm, knowing her careful effort was noticed.

grounding: A child says a quick thanks and then feels real gratitude on seeing the effort behind a neighbour's favour.

passage:
When I got jaundice in Class 5 and missed three weeks of school, I thought I'd fail everything. Then every Friday, Maria came to our gate with a plastic folder. She had copied all the notes by hand for me, in blue ink with red headings, even the diagrams.
I just said "thanks" the first time. Then Mummy showed me the date at the top of one page: Maria had written it at eleven at night.
When I went back to school, I didn't know how to say thank you properly. So I spent Sunday teaching her how to bowl a leg-spinner, which she'd been begging me about for months. She got it on the fifteenth try and screamed.
Now she bowls better than me.
- Lalit

qa.q: What colour ink did Maria use for the headings?
qa.a: Red headings.

qa.q: What did Lalit feel on seeing the date at the top of the page?
qa.a: Lalit probably felt surprised and moved, realising Maria had stayed up until eleven at night to copy the notes.

qa.q: Which choice worked as a way of saying thank you, and why?
qa.a: Teaching Maria the leg-spinner she had wanted for months worked, because it returned the favour with real time and effort, not just a word.

qa.q: How might Maria see the bowling lesson?
qa.a: Maria likely felt delighted and thanked in return, seeing Lalit give time to help her with something she cared about.

grounding: The narrator looks back on a friend's effort and returns the favour, showing gratitude beyond a quick phrase.

passage:
Coach's note, Tuesday, junior cricket camp
This morning Deepak arrived early and saw Lakshmi Amma, our groundskeeper, watering the pitch with a heavy pipe before sunrise. He asked her why. She told him the pitch cracks if it isn't watered twice a day.
After practice, Deepak stayed back. He picked up stray balls, rolled them into the basket, and then went up to Lakshmi Amma. He said, "Thank you for our pitch. I didn't know you come so early." She looked surprised, then smiled.
I did not tell him to do this. I have asked him to share at tomorrow's team huddle what he learned, so the others also see the work behind the ground.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi Amma say happens if the pitch isn't watered?
qa.a: It cracks.

qa.q: What might Deepak have been feeling when he thanked Lakshmi Amma?
qa.a: Deepak likely felt grateful and a bit surprised, now seeing the hard work behind the pitch he used every day.

qa.q: How could the coach help the whole team learn from Deepak?
qa.a: By asking Deepak to share at the huddle, the coach helps others notice the effort behind the ground, not just say thanks by habit.

qa.q: What was it like for Lakshmi Amma to be thanked?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and pleased, perhaps because her early work usually goes unseen.

grounding: A coach's note shows a child saying thank you after seeing the real effort behind a service.

passage:
Thursday
When I was down with fever last week, Sahil from next door copied out all the science notes for me. I thought he'd just photocopied them, so I said "thanks" the way you say thanks for passing the salt. Today his mother told Mummy he stayed up two nights writing them, and he even drew the diagram of the ear in three colours. My face went hot. My tiny thanks felt so small next to that. So after tea I made him a proper card: "Thank you for the three-colour ear. I know it took two whole nights." And since he's hopeless at Hindi, I told him I'd help him practise his poem recitation on Saturday. He grinned and pretended it was nothing.
Avni

qa.q: Which diagram did Sahil draw in three colours?
qa.a: The diagram of the ear.

qa.q: Why did Avni's face go hot?
qa.a: Avni felt embarrassed and a bit guilty that a quick 'thanks' didn't match the two nights of effort behind the notes.

qa.q: What turned Avni's rote thanks into real gratitude?
qa.a: Learning about the effort, naming it specifically in a card, and returning the favour by helping with the Hindi poem 🙂

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt reading the card?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt pleased and appreciated that his effort was noticed, even while pretending it was nothing.

grounding: It illustrates a child moving from a rote thank-you to real gratitude after seeing the effort behind a kindness, and returning the favour.
